what confounds affect H2-H1 opponent scoring delta
how to test reliability of a team defensive trait

historical_evidence.finding: Connector quality Q_p split-half reliability (player-season level, halves) showed r=0.215, Spearman-Brown 0.355, ICC 0.216; 78.4% of variance within-player half-to-half. The question was untestable: Q_p cannot be treated as a stable scoutable trait.

Ranked playsheet counter ranking (BEST vs AVOID) tested on 10 playoff series; full-rank Spearman not significant; pairwise BEST > AVOID had some signal but limited by small sample, leakage, and nonstationarity risks.

Foul-trouble sequencing after star 2nd foul: headline +0.204 PPP on next possessions was caused by free-throw possessions (41.8% vs 9.9%); excluding them, no significant effect. Artifact due to mechanical inclusion of free throws.

Possession Control Index incremental R² over ORtg in explaining Net Rating was driven by a leakage term that tracked DRtg (corr +0.894); offensive-control components added only +0.005. Artifact from outcome containing defense by construction.

failed_approaches.what_failed: split-half reliability of a half-based on-off PPP metric at player level
failed_approaches.why: low measurement reliability; most variance was within-player across halves, making the trait untestable

failed_approaches.what_failed: using raw next-possession PPP without excluding free-throw trips to measure a defensive effect
failed_approaches.why: artifact from free-throw possessions mechanically inflating the apparent effect

failed_approaches.what_failed: adding a possession control index to ORtg to explain Net Rating
failed_approaches.why: leakage: the index correlated with DRtg (+0.894), which is already part of Net Rating by construction

evidence_establishes: Half-based metrics (on-off PPP gap per half) can have very low split-half reliability at the player level, with most variance within-player (SF-APPS-085).
Halftime-to-halftime scoring changes can be misleading if mechanical components (free throws, pace) are not properly handled (SF15).
Metrics that aim to capture defensive traits can become artifacts when they inadvertently correlate with the defensive component of the outcome (SF-APPS-068).
Playoff-level counter rankings suffer from small sample and nonstationarity, making full-rank validation difficult (SF-APPS-018).
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether a defense's effect on opponent H2-H1 change is a reliable team trait; no direct test of this question has been retrieved.
The reliability of any team-level H2-H1 delta metric, either within or across seasons.
The magnitude of true team defensive adjustment ability, if any, beyond random noise and regression to the mean.
own_inferences: If a player-level half-based metric is too noisy to be reliable, a team-level metric aggregated over many possessions may still be noisy but could benefit from larger within-unit sample; however, many confounds remain.

The experience of SF-APPS-085 suggests that reliability of halftime adjustment metrics is likely low even at team level, because half-to-half scoring variance is dominated by random factors and opponent adjustments that are specific to each game.

Regression to the mean is a major confound: teams with extreme H1 opponent scoring will naturally have less extreme H2 scoring, creating a spurious negative H2-H1 delta that may masquerade as a 'defensive adjustment' trait if not modelled.
Coaching changes, roster turnover, and season-to-season nonstationarity (DRIFT) further threaten any attempt to measure a stable team trait across multiple seasons.

The available 120 team-seasons (roughly 4 seasons × 30 teams) provide a moderate sample for a team-level ICC, but power would be insufficient if true ICC is below 0.1–0.15, which is plausible given SF-APPS-085.
uncertainties: No direct historical test exists, so all inferences about testability draw from analogous but distinct player-level and different-metric studies.
The true between-team variance in H2-H1 opponent scoring adjustment is unknown; it might be zero or small.
It is unclear whether an adequate control for opponent offensive strength and game script can fully remove confounding, given the observational nature of the data.

historical_effect.explanation: The split-half reliability failure for connector Q_p (FAM:SF-APPS-085) demonstrates that halftime-based metrics suffer from severe measurement noise and low stability, making it unlikely that a defensive H2-H1 adjustment trait can be reliably measured without a very large sample and careful confound control. This evidence shifted the decision from 'proceed' to 'do_not_proceed' because the risk of an untestable or artifact-laden result is too high given the data and design constraints.

blocking_constraints.text: Half-based scoring deltas likely have high within-team variance and low signal-to-noise ratio, as seen in analogous player-level split-half failures (SF-APPS-085).

Opponent quality, game location, rest, injuries, and within-game script (e.g., blowout slowdowns) confound the H2-H1 delta, and regression to the mean creates a mechanical negative correlation with H1 scoring that is not a defensive trait.
Teams, coaches, and rosters change across seasons, so a trait measured across multiple seasons may not be stable, undermining the concept of a persistent team trait.

prior_work.summary: No earlier study has directly tested whether the team defensive effect on opponent H2-H1 change is a reliable trait. The most relevant prior work (FAM:SF-APPS-085) found that a player-level half-based metric was untestable due to low reliability, warning that similar halftime-based traits may be too noisy to measure.

risks.text: The outcome (opponent H2-H1 points/PPP change) is subject to large game-to-game variance and measurement noise, likely yielding low intraclass correlation at the team-season level.

Confounders include opponent offensive quality, home-court advantage, rest days, in-game foul trouble of key players, and game script (e.g., a large lead leading to relaxed defense). These must be modeled and may still leave residual confounding.

Regression to the mean is a severe risk: teams that allow unusually high (or low) H1 scoring will tend to see H2 scoring shift towards the mean, creating an apparent 'adjustment' that is purely statistical and not a defensive trait.
Defensive systems and personnel change between seasons and even within a season, so any estimated trait may not replicate across time windows, limiting practical utility.
120 team-seasons may be insufficient to detect a small true team-year ICC, especially after controlling for confounders and partitioning variance appropriately.

design.estimand: The within-season split-half reliability (ICC) of a team's defensive halftime adjustment metric, defined as the opponent's points per possession (PPP) change from H1 to H2, adjusted for opponent offensive rating, game location, and rest, and corrected for regression to the mean using an empirical Bayes or random-effects approach.
design.unit: Team-season (30 teams per season × 4 seasons = 120 team-seasons), with games as repeated measures within each team-season.
design.sample: All regular-season games from NBA 2022-23 through 2025-26 (approximately 82 games per team-season). Split each team-season into two halves by game order (odd/even game IDs) to compute split-half reliability.
design.power: Monte Carlo simulation assuming true ICC of 0.05–0.15, 41 games per half per team-season, 120 team-seasons; power would be inadequate (likely < 50%) to reject ICC=0 at conventional thresholds without large sample augmentation.
design.controls: Fixed effects or pre-adjustment for opponent offensive efficiency (e.g., season-long offensive rating), home/away, rest days (back-to-backs), in-game score differential at halftime (to model regression to the mean), and interaction terms as needed.
design.falsification: Test whether the same analysis on randomized team labels or on H1-H1 split (i.e., substituting H2-H1 with a fake delta between two halves of H1) still shows a 'trait' – it should not. Also, test whether the estimated team adjustments predict future season halves out of sample.
design.multiplicity: Pre-specify a single primary outcome metric (adjusted opponent PPP delta) and one reliability index (ICC). Any exploratory analyses will be flagged as secondary.
design.decision_rule: Conclude that the trait is reliable if the split-half ICC exceeds 0.20 with a lower 95% confidence bound above 0.10, and if the falsification tests pass. Otherwise, declare the trait untestable or not reliably measurable.
design.data_version: NBA stats API per-game play-by-play and box-score data from 2022-23 through 2025-26 regular season, with derived possession counts and PPP. Dataset frozen as of 2026-10-06.

You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.
